title: BRAC study: most Dhaka battery-rickshaw drivers are migrants, 96% unlicensed
excerpt: A BRAC and BIGD survey of 450 drivers found 78% in Dhaka came from other districts, 96% had no licence and nearly 63% could not support their families for more than a week without income.

image.alt: File photo: battery-run easy-bike auto-rickshaws parked along a road in Khulna
image.credit: File photo: TanvirSdq / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
Most battery-powered rickshaw drivers in Dhaka are migrants from other districts, and almost none hold a licence, according to a study by BRAC and the BRAC Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD). The findings were presented at a policy dialogue at the CIRDAP auditorium in Dhaka on Tuesday (24 November), Prothom Alo English and the Financial Express reported.

Mehnaz Rabbani, BIGD's director of operations, presented the findings, Prothom Alo reported. The study surveyed 450 drivers in Dhaka and Barishal in June and July. It found that 78.3% of the drivers surveyed in Dhaka had come from other districts, and 84.2% of them had moved because of limited jobs and income where they lived.

Drivers earn an average of Tk 29,000 a month and pay owners an average of Tk 10,323 in rent, or 38.6% of their earnings, the study found. About 78% rent their rickshaws. In the previous year, 42.2% had faced a major livelihood crisis, and most of them said their income fell by more than half or stopped. Nearly 62.9% said they could not support their families for more than a week if their income stopped. In May, 26.7% had been involved in at least one road accident.

Some 96% of drivers had no licence, and two-thirds had been fined or harassed at some point, the Financial Express reported. The study warned that a sudden ban or restrictions could cut drivers' incomes and hurt their families. It called the Local Government Division's E-Rickshaw Movement Rules, 2026 an important step but said implementation would be the main challenge. It recommended safety standards, designated roads and speeds, safe charging at garages, and a system to collect and recycle old batteries.

BRAC Executive Director Asif Saleh called for a three-to-four-year transition plan to limit the impact on drivers' livelihoods, the Financial Express reported. Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan said, "We are not against auto-rickshaws or rickshaw drivers. Their right to a livelihood must also be protected," according to Prothom Alo. Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Abdus Salam called for an integrated plan based on the city's overall capacity.

Why it matters

Battery rickshaws are a large source of work for poor rural migrants with few other options. Any crackdown or new licensing rules will hit households with almost no savings. The data give NGOs working on urban poverty, migration, road safety and battery waste evidence to argue for a gradual, livelihood-based approach.

What to watch

How the city corporations and the Local Government Division put the 2026 rules into effect, whether licensing begins, and whether any transition support is offered to drivers. The full study had not been posted online at the time of writing; Devlens relied on press reports.
